current_answer: AI-exposed work may be paying more while opening fewer junior doors. A new U.S. job-posting analysis finds advertised pay rose faster in highly AI-exposed occupations, while the entry-level share of their postings fell from 29% to 10% between 2021 and 2026. That does not prove AI caused either pattern: the analysis uses exposure, not employer adoption, and a shift toward senior roles can lift advertised pay. It changes the evidence map by showing why a pay headline cannot dismiss the entry-route warning. Texas graduate records still show lower first-year employment and earnings in more-exposed majors, while Yale’s broad U.S. monitor still finds no clear economy-wide footprint. The live risk is uneven restructuring and a harder entry route in some settings, not demonstrated AI mass unemployment.

catalogue_card.question: Can AI-exposed jobs pay more and still be harder to enter?
catalogue_card.text: A new U.S. posting analysis finds faster advertised-pay growth in highly AI-exposed work, while entry-level openings make up a much smaller share of its ads. It tracks exposure and posted jobs, not employer adoption, actual pay or your odds.

summary: Indeed Hiring Lab analyzed millions of U.S. postings with advertised salaries. Pay in the most AI-exposed occupations rose about 46% from 2021 to mid-2026, compared with 25% in the least-exposed group.
The same postings show a marked seniority shift in the most-exposed occupations: entry-level ads fell from 29% to 10% of that group’s postings, while senior ads rose from 22% to 47%.

This is not proof that AI caused a wage gain or the junior shift. The analysis uses occupational exposure, and holding seniority mix constant reduces the post-ChatGPT pay estimate to 2.4%, which is not statistically significant.

The result changes the entry-level evidence map: advertised pay can rise while the first rung shrinks. Texas graduate records, U.S. graduate unemployment data and Yale’s broad monitor still measure different outcomes and do not cancel one another.
uncertainty: Indeed measures advertised U.S. jobs with salaries and an occupational exposure score, not actual wages, employer AI deployment, hires, layoffs or a personal outcome.
The exposure-linked advertised-pay premium falls when seniority composition is held constant, and that most-controlled estimate is not statistically significant.
Texas graduate records, job postings and Yale’s broad monitor cover different populations and outcomes; together they do not establish a national causal effect or a personal forecast.
freshness_note: Checked 25 September 2026. A new U.S. advertised-pay and seniority analysis changes the structure-of-work evidence; it does not settle AI causation, realized pay or an economy-wide employment effect.
